opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so this is something my students and I spent a lot of time on, and it led to the paper we called "Are Emergent Abilities of Large Language Models a Mirage?" The short version of my take is that a lot of what's been described as emergence, these sharp, unpredictable jumps in capability as you scale models, is at least partly a product of how we measure performance, not necessarily something fundamental changing inside the model.

Here's the intuition. If you look at the underlying quantity the model is optimized for, something like per-token loss or the probability it assigns to the correct answer, that tends to improve fairly smoothly and predictably with scale. The scaling-law literature shows this quite nicely. But many benchmarks that people pointed to as showing emergence use metrics that are very harsh and nonlinear. Exact match is the classic example. If you need to get every token of a multi-digit arithmetic answer exactly right, then even if the per-token accuracy is creeping up steadily, the probability of getting the whole sequence right stays near zero for a long time and then shoots up. So you see this hockey-stick curve and say, "Wow, a new ability just appeared," when in fact the model was getting steadily better the whole way.

We tested this in a few ways. First, we took the same model outputs and just changed the metric, from exact match to something continuous like token edit distance, or from multiple-choice accuracy to Brier score, and a lot of the sharp transitions became smooth and predictable. Second, we did a kind of meta-analysis across BIG-bench and found that the claimed emergent abilities clustered overwhelmingly on a small number of discontinuous metrics. And third, we showed you could go the other way: take vision models, where nobody really claimed emergence, and by choosing a sufficiently harsh metric you can manufacture what looks like an emergent ability. That last one, I think, was pretty convincing to people that the metric matters a lot.

There's also a resolution issue. If you only evaluate a handful of model sizes on a small test set, you just don't have the statistical resolution to see the small but nonzero performance in smaller models, so it looks like zero and then suddenly not zero.

Now, I want to be careful about what we're not saying. We're not saying large models don't have impressive capabilities, or that nothing qualitatively interesting ever happens with scale. And we're not saying the metrics people care about are wrong. Sometimes you really do care about exact match; if you want the arithmetic answer, partial credit doesn't help you. The point is more about prediction and science. If you want to forecast when a capability will show up, which matters a lot for planning and for safety, you should look at the smoother underlying quantities, because those are much more predictable. The "unpredictability" is often in the lens, not in the model.

So my assessment is: the claim that these abilities are inherently unpredictable is overstated. With the right measurements, a lot of it becomes forecastable, and I think that's actually good news, both for the science and for anyone worried about being surprised by what the next model can do.

r001.rationale: The response explains that steadily improving per-token accuracy raises the probability of getting an entire sequence correct, even when exact-match performance appears to jump suddenly.

r002.rationale: It says many apparent emergent abilities become smooth and predictable with suitable measurements, so their unpredictability is overstated.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so this is something we spent a lot of time on, and I'd say the short version is that I'm fairly skeptical of the strong form of that claim. The claim, as it's usually stated, is that as you scale models up, there are these abilities that appear suddenly and unpredictably — they're essentially absent at one scale and then present at the next, and you couldn't have seen it coming by extrapolating from smaller models. And that framing has had a lot of influence, both on how people think about scaling and, frankly, on how people think about safety and risk.

What we argued in our work is that a lot of that apparent emergence is actually an artifact of how we measure things, not a property of the model itself. If you look at the specific benchmarks where emergence has been claimed, they're overwhelmingly evaluated with metrics that are discontinuous or nonlinear — things like exact match accuracy or multiple-choice grading, where you get zero credit unless every token in a sequence is correct. And if you think about it, if a model's per-token error rate is improving smoothly with scale, then the probability of getting an entire multi-token answer exactly right goes like that per-token probability raised to the length of the sequence. That's going to look flat for a long time and then shoot up. So the sharpness is coming from the metric, not from some phase transition inside the model.

What we did was fairly simple. We took the same models, the same tasks, and just swapped in metrics that are continuous — things like token edit distance, or looking at the log-likelihood of the correct answer — and the emergence largely disappears. You get smooth, predictable curves. And we took it a step further and showed you can manufacture emergence in a setting where everyone agrees nothing special is happening — vision models, where nobody was claiming emergent abilities — just by choosing a harsh enough metric. So it's a very reproducible phenomenon, but it's reproducible as a measurement effect.

Now, I want to be careful here, because I don't think this means nothing interesting happens at scale. There's a weaker version of the claim that I think is totally defensible — that there are capabilities that are hard to anticipate in practice, especially when you're looking at downstream behavior in the world rather than a benchmark number. And there's a related issue, which is that a lot of these evaluations have very small test sets, so you have a resolution problem — you literally can't see the smooth improvement because you don't have enough samples to estimate a small probability. That's a real limitation, but again, it's a limitation of our evaluation infrastructure.

So my assessment is: unpredictable in the sense of fundamentally discontinuous, I don't buy it, and I think the evidence points the other way. Unpredictable in the sense that we often fail to measure carefully enough to predict — yes, absolutely, and that's a call to do better science around evaluation rather than to treat these systems as inherently mysterious. I actually think that distinction matters a lot for policy conversations, because "we can't possibly know what the next model will do" leads you to a very different place than "we need better instruments."

r001.rationale: The response explains that smoothly improving per-token accuracy predicts exact-sequence success, whose probability compounds across tokens and can make performance on all-or-nothing metrics rise sharply.

r002.rationale: It argues that apparent emergence in many studied benchmarks is a measurement effect and that continuous metrics reveal smooth, predictable performance curves.

astra-6.text:
I think we have to be careful about what we mean by unpredictable. Do we mean that an ability appears suddenly on a particular benchmark, or that we couldn’t have anticipated it from what smaller models were doing? Those aren’t necessarily the same thing.

Imagine a task where you only get credit if the entire answer is correct. A model might be improving gradually, but the score stays close to zero until it crosses a threshold. Then the benchmark makes that gradual improvement look like a sudden emergence. If you measure partial progress, you might see a much smoother curve.

That doesn’t mean every emergent ability is a measurement artifact, or that we can predict everything a larger model will do. It means the stronger claim—that these abilities are inherently unpredictable—needs more evidence. I’d want to know what we measured, what information was available beforehand, and whether we actually tried to make a prediction. Something being surprising to us is different from it being unpredictable.

r001.rationale: It explains how all-or-nothing scoring can make gradual improvement look sudden, but does not connect expected sequence-prediction behavior to predicting performance.

r002.rationale: It questions the claim that abilities are inherently unpredictable, but does not argue that many studied emergent abilities are fairly predictable.

sol-6.1.text:
I think we have to be careful about what we mean by unpredictable. There’s a difference between saying we don’t yet have a good way to predict when a capability will appear and saying that it’s fundamentally impossible to predict.

One issue is how we measure the capability. If you use a metric where the model gets credit only when the entire answer is correct, you can see what looks like a sudden jump. But underneath that, the model may have been improving gradually. Once it crosses the threshold your metric cares about, you call that emergence. If you measure partial progress, the picture can look much smoother.

That doesn’t mean every emergent ability is an artifact, or that we can now predict everything these models will do. It means that an apparent discontinuity in a benchmark isn’t, by itself, evidence of an unpredictable change in the model. We need to look at the measurement and then ask what we can actually forecast.

r001.rationale: The response explains how all-or-nothing metrics can make gradual improvement look sudden, but it does not say that expected sequence-prediction behavior predicts performance on those metrics.

r002.rationale: The response says apparent benchmark discontinuities alone do not prove unpredictability, but it does not claim that many studied emergent abilities are fairly predictable.
